content.title: A Week on Pager Is a Design Flaw, Not a Tradition
content.text:
The week-long on-call rotation is so common that most engineers have never questioned it. One person carries the pager for seven days, hands it off, and recovers. It feels fair because it is symmetrical. I think it is one of the worst-designed practices in the industry, and that the data, where teams have bothered to collect it, points clearly toward shorter shifts distributed across time zones.

Start with what a week of on-call does to the person carrying it. The Lindqvist Group's 2025 survey of 1,860 engineers at companies with formal incident processes asked respondents to rate their sleep quality, their ability to concentrate on planned work, and their intention to remain in their role over the next year, separately for on-call weeks and normal weeks. On on-call weeks, 61 percent reported sleep they described as poor or very poor, against 14 percent on normal weeks. Self-reported focused work fell by a median of 12 hours over the week. And 27 percent of respondents on weekly rotations said on-call was a significant factor in considering leaving, compared with 9 percent among respondents whose shifts were twelve hours or shorter.

Those figures would matter even if incident response were unaffected. It is not. The Ostrava Reliability Consortium, which pools anonymised incident data from 34 companies, published a comparison in early 2026 of mean time to resolve for incidents that paged during the responder's first 24 hours on shift versus their fifth day or later. Median MTTR for the first-day group was 38 minutes. For the fifth-day-or-later group it was 57 minutes. The consortium's authors were careful to note that the later-week incidents were not measurably more severe by their own scoring, and that the gap held when they controlled for time of day. Their explanation was the obvious one: a responder woken twice already that week is slower, makes more mistakes reading dashboards, and is more likely to escalate incorrectly.

The alternative is not complicated. Shifts of eight to twelve hours, handed off with a short written summary, and placed so that each shift falls in its responder's working day. A team spread across three regions can cover the clock with nobody paged at night. A team in one region can still shorten shifts and accept that some nights are covered by people who volunteered for them with compensation, rather than by whoever's turn it was.

Tomasz Ferreira, a staff engineer, ran this change at a 90-person infrastructure company. Before, two teams of six ran weekly rotations. After, the same twelve people covered two eight-hour regional shifts plus a paid overnight shift on a separate volunteer roster. Over the following two quarters he tracked a 31 percent drop in MTTR, a fall in pages that were acknowledged late from 18 percent to 3 percent, and, in the team's own quarterly survey, a rise in the proportion of engineers describing on-call as manageable from 40 percent to 85 percent. He was clear that some of the MTTR improvement came from the handoff document, which forced each shift to write down what was flaky, rather than from the schedule itself.

There are costs, and I do not want to wave them away. Follow-the-sun requires people in more than one time zone, which a small single-office team simply does not have. Handoffs lose context; an incident that spans a shift boundary can be slower, not faster, and the Ostrava data shows a modest penalty of about 6 minutes for incidents that crossed a handoff. Shorter shifts mean more of them, and more schedule administration. And weekly rotations do have one genuine advantage: the on-call engineer accumulates enough context over the week to notice patterns that a fresh responder would miss.

Still, the balance is not close. We already accept that a pilot or a surgeon should not work a seven-day shift because tired people make worse decisions. Incident response is not different in kind. It is just a place where we have historically measured the cost in other people's sleep rather than in our own numbers. Once teams start collecting those numbers, the week-long pager tends not to survive the first review.

notes: Opinion piece arguing weekly on-call should be replaced by short follow-the-sun shifts, citing fictional burnout survey percentages and MTTR comparisons plus a named engineer's before/after numbers, with acknowledged costs. Judge should see a specific operational argument backed by figures, not a generic burnout complaint.
